conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is supported by strong randomized-trial evidence specifically for postmenopausal women at elevated risk. Therefore, it strongly endorses the claim.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported by strong randomized-trial evidence, with an important qualification: the evidence applies to *postmenopausal women at moderately increased/high risk*, not to average-risk women.

The pivotal placebo-controlled MAP.3 trial found that exemestane significantly lowered invasive breast-cancer incidence. Reported annual rates were 0.19% with exemestane versus 0.55% with placebo—about a **65% relative reduction** (11 versus 32 invasive cancers; hazard ratio 0.35 in the published trial). The trial’s median follow-up was about 3 years, so it directly demonstrates fewer diagnoses over that period, not a proven reduction in breast-cancer mortality or the full long-term balance of benefits and harms.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507

NCI’s prevention evidence summary likewise concludes that, in high-risk postmenopausal women, three years of exemestane reduced breast-cancer incidence by 65% versus controls.  
https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/hp/breast-prevention-pdq

Clinical decision-making still requires individualized risk–benefit assessment. Aromatase inhibitors can cause small-to-moderate harms; unlike tamoxifen, they do not have the same thromboembolic/endometrial-cancer risks, but musculoskeletal symptoms and bone effects are relevant concerns. USPSTF concludes the net benefit is greater as baseline breast-cancer risk rises.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction
